title: TCP/IP and the network stack
subtitle: Learn how bytes really move between two machines, so you can read network errors and stop paying for handshakes you do not need.

IP can lose, repeat and reorder packets. TCP hides this from you, but the hiding costs time: a handshake to start, and waiting when a packet is lost. Most "network problems" in a backend are about those costs.

What TCP adds on top of IP

Every byte has a sequence number. TCP finds lost data through these numbers and errors through checksums, then sends the data again
Each packet TCP sends carries a window: how many more bytes the receiver will accept right now
. A slow reader makes a fast sender wait.
TCP must slow down when the network looks overloaded, so the network does not collapse
Why a new connection costs a round trip

Your app cannot send the request until the handshake ends. That is one full round trip with no useful data. If a round trip to the server takes 150 ms, you wait about 150 ms before the request even leaves.

q.v: and gets "connection refused" at once. What is the most likely cause?

options.v: The network dropped every packet on the way.
The machine answered, but no program is listening on port 8080.
The server is up but slow, and took too long to answer.

why.v: A refusal is a fast reset (RST) from the machine. TCP answers a SYN that matches no connection with an RST. Dropped packets give a timeout instead.

q.v: Before an HTTP request can go out on a brand-new TCP connection, what must happen first?

options.v: Nothing. TCP sends the request in the first packet.
The three-way handshake, which costs one round trip.
A DNS lookup for every packet.

why.v: SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK must finish before the request is sent. With TLS on top, there is more waiting. Reusing an open connection skips all of it.

q.v: Ten requests share one HTTP/2 connection over TCP. One packet is lost. What happens?

options.v: Only the request in that packet waits.
All ten requests stall until the lost packet is sent again.
The connection closes and all requests fail.

why.v: TCP delivers bytes in order and cannot see HTTP/2 streams, so every stream waits. QUIC (used by HTTP/3) blocks only the streams in the lost packet.

q.v: Your pooled connections go through an AWS NAT gateway. After a quiet night, the first calls fail with "connection reset". What is a good fix?

options.v: Turn on TCP keep-alive with an interval under 350 seconds, or close idle pooled connections sooner.
Open a new connection for every request forever.
Raise the request timeout to 5 minutes.

why.v: The NAT gateway forgets connections idle for 350 seconds and answers later packets with RST. Keep-alives or a shorter pool idle time stop you from using a forgotten connection.

q.v: Which of these does TCP give you, but plain UDP does not?

options.v: Ordered delivery and sending lost data again.

why.v: UDP also has ports and a checksum, but it does not promise delivery or order. TCP adds connections, ordering, retransmission, flow control and congestion control.
